setting: A short lecture in an introductory psychology class about how sleep stages relate to memory.
narrator_intro: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Many students think sleep is just “time off” for the brain. Research suggests the opposite.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: During a normal night, we cycle through light sleep, deep sleep, and REM sleep several times.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Deep sleep seems especially important for stabilizing factual memories—the kind you need for dates, definitions, and formulas.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: REM sleep, when most dreaming occurs, appears more linked to integrating ideas and practicing skills.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: If you cut sleep short, you often lose more REM toward morning, which can hurt problem-solving the next day.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: That is one reason an all-nighter can leave you able to recognize a term but unable to apply it on an essay.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Naps help a little, but they rarely replace a full set of night cycles.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Caffeine can make you feel alert without restoring the memory processes that happen during sleep.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: So for exam weeks, consistent sleep may matter as much as another hour of review.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Next lecture we'll look at experiments that tested sleep and vocabulary learning in adults.

narrator_outro: Now get ready to answer the questions.

questions.narrator_text: What is the talk mainly about?

options.text: How to avoid all deep sleep permanently
How to brew stronger coffee before exams
How sleep stages support different kinds of memory

questions.explanation: The professor links deep sleep and REM sleep to different memory functions and study outcomes.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—caffeine is mentioned only as something that does not replace sleep processes.
questions.correctAnswer: How sleep stages support different kinds of memory

questions.narrator_text: According to the professor, what is deep sleep especially important for?

options.text: Stabilizing factual memories such as dates and definitions

questions.explanation: He says deep sleep seems especially important for stabilizing factual memories like dates, definitions, and formulas.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing D—sleep supports memory; it does not replace study.
questions.correctAnswer: Stabilizing factual memories such as dates and definitions

questions.narrator_text: What often happens if sleep is cut short?

options.text: People gain extra deep sleep at sunrise
More REM sleep toward morning is lost, which can hurt problem-solving
Factual memory improves without any REM
Naps automatically become a full night of sleep

questions.explanation: Cutting sleep short often reduces later REM, which can hurt problem-solving the next day.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—he does not say deep sleep increases when sleep is shortened.
questions.correctAnswer: More REM sleep toward morning is lost, which can hurt problem-solving

questions.narrator_text: What does the professor suggest about caffeine?

options.text: It fully restores memory processes lost from missing sleep
It is required before every psychology exam
It can increase alertness without restoring sleep-related memory processes
It only works during REM sleep

questions.explanation: He says caffeine can make you feel alert without restoring the memory processes that happen during sleep.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—that is what he warns against assuming.
questions.correctAnswer: It can increase alertness without restoring sleep-related memory processes
